summary:
We developed ARES III, an interactive browser-based mission trainer for kids ages 7–12 where a five-specialist crew must keep a Martian outpost alive across three Sols.

The game addresses the challenge by turning real deep-space engineering constraints into tangible, replayable mechanics where no choice is free. Every action displays an explicit resource trade-off—such as spending limited power to produce oxygen, sheltering in a dark radiation bunker, or voting as a crew to switch to flashlights to save energy. Gameplay is grounded in real NASA open data: live NASA DONKI space weather scales solar storm intensity, NASA OSDR informs radiation dosimetry, and Mars InSight/Perseverance data models day-night power cycles and dust accumulation, all transparently cited in an in-game "Science for Judges" panel.

Space STEM content often oversimplifies survival or overwhelms young learners. Requiring zero downloads or accounts, and playable solo with AI bots or in real-time multiplayer, ARES III bridges that gap—teaching kids how real NASA mission planners prioritize under pressure.
details:
HOW IT WORKS

ARES III is a browser-based cooperative survival and resource-management game designed for junior astronauts ages 7–12. Up to five players—or a solo player teamed up with four AI bots—take on specialized crew roles (Captain, Botanist, Engineer, Scientist, and Communications Officer) to keep a Martian outpost operational across three Martian days (Sols, 100 seconds each).

To win, the crew must complete two rounds of role-specific tasks (20 total) across 34 interactive stations featuring 12 distinct skill minigames (such as aligning communication waves, cleaning dust off solar panels, repairing valves, and scanning rock samples) while transmitting 100% of mission data back to Earth. Meanwhile, players must keep three core survival bars from hitting zero: Power, Life Support, and Radiation Shielding.

Every action enforces an explicit engineering trade-off shown directly on screen (e.g., "SPEND: -8% Power -> GAIN: +25% Life Support"). Dynamic events force real-time teamwork: random anomalies (water leaks, electrical shorts, CO2 spikes) drain resources until repaired, and periodic Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) solar storms force the crew to shelter in an underground radiation bunker—sacrificing visibility for 8 seconds—or risk lethal radiation doses. At the end of each Sol, or when power drops below 50%, the crew holds live votes (such as switching to flashlights to save 70% power at the cost of darkness).

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT

Space STEM materials for children often stay too abstract or oversimplify survival. ARES III makes real NASA mission-planning constraints tangible in intense 7-to-8-minute sessions. Players walk away understanding that no resource in deep space is free, how solar weather affects radiation exposure, and why astronauts must prioritize competing systems under pressure. Because it runs directly in any desktop or mobile browser with zero downloads or accounts required, it lowers barriers for home play, families, and classroom STEM activities.

CREATIVITY & DESIGN FACTORS CONSIDERED

Rather than building a passive dashboard, we combined accessible top-down character customization and fast-paced minigames with authentic NASA science. To avoid overwhelming 7–12-year-olds, we distilled outpost survival into three intuitive vital bars while translating technical terms (such as Sols and radiation dosimetry) into clear visual feedback. High replayability comes from randomized tasks, anomalies, and variable storm intensities.

TOOLS, SOFTWARE & NASA DATA USED

- Frontend & Game Engine: Built as a lightweight web application using HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript, and CSS for cross-platform browser and mobile touch-joystick compatibility.

- Multiplayer & AI: Powered by Firebase for real-time room matchmaking (public lobbies and 4-letter private room codes) and state synchronization, alongside autonomous AI bots for single-player mode.

- Real NASA Open Data: Integrates the NASA DONKI API to scale in-game CME solar storm severity based on real solar flare activity, NASA OSDR research to model radiation dosimetry and shielding mechanics, and Mars InSight/Perseverance environmental findings for day/night solar generation drops and panel dust accumulation. An in-game "Science for Judges" panel transparently documents every dataset used.
